extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate mathematics students (discrete mathematics / proof techniques)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and criteria for constructing and checking proofs by (ordinary) induction, strong induction, and proof by smallest counterexample, plus criteria for checking relation properties (reflexive, symmetric, transitive). Intended as a how-to reference for writing correct proofs in elementary discrete mathematics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Outline for Proof by Mathematical Induction
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove a family of statements S_n for every n in N, prove a base case (usually S_1) and prove that S_k implies S_{k+1}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a direct proof in the inductive step: assume S_k is true and manipulate algebraically (or otherwise) to derive S_{k+1}. Check the base case(s) explicitly. Many examples illustrate multiplying both sides, adding quantities, or substituting known equalities when moving from S_k to S_{k+1}. Note: this standard outline proves statements for n > = the base index (typically n>0).

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitation of Ordinary Induction on Z (two-sided index sets)
rubrics_metrics.description: The standard induction outline (show S_1 and S_k=>S_{k+1}) only yields S_n for n >= 1; it does not establish statements for n in Z (including 0 or negative indices).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you must prove ∀n ∈ Z, S_n by induction, you must (in addition to a forward step) provide a way to move backwards (e.g., show S_k => S_{k-1}) or show some S_a is true and both S_k⇒S_{k+1} and S_k⇒S_{k-1}. Be explicit about which indices are covered by your base cases so the induction 'dominoes' do not 'run off the end.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of algebraic/inequality manipulations in inductive step
rubrics_metrics.description: When the inductive step involves algebraic expressions or inequalities, perform justified algebraic manipulations (e.g., multiply both sides by positive quantities, add equal quantities, or remove positive terms) to transform S_k into S_{k+1}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be careful with operations that could change inequality directions (e.g., multiplying by negative numbers). The text emphasizes the oft-forgotten fact about inequalities: you may add unequal quantities to both sides while preserving order provided the greater side receives the greater addend (if x<y and a<b then x+a<y+b), and multiplying by a positive factor preserves inequalities. Use such legitimate maneuvers to derive the next case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Outline for Proof by Strong Induction
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove S_n for all n ∈ N by strong induction: (1) Prove the first statement S_1 (or the first several S_i); (2) For any k>1, assume S_1 ∧ S_2 ∧ ... ∧ S_k and prove this implies S_{k+1}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strong induction allows you to use any or all earlier cases (S_1 through S_k) to deduce S_{k+1}. Use strong induction when S_k alone does not neatly force S_{k+1}, but some earlier S_m (m<k) does. Ensure you establish enough initial base cases so the induction hypothesis covers the indices needed (e.g., in examples one checks the first six cases).

rubrics_metrics.name: When to choose strong induction vs ordinary induction
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose strong induction when the implication S_k ⇒ S_{k+1} is hard or impossible to derive directly but S_{k - i} (or several earlier statements) collectively imply S_{k+1}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: divisibility properties where algebraic expansion of (k+1)th term won't factor the modulus cleanly from the S_k assumption alone, or recursive sequences (like Fibonacci) where F_{n} depends on two earlier terms. In such cases, assuming all prior statements up to k gives the flexibility needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Outline for Proof by Smallest Counterexample
rubrics_metrics.description: Proof by smallest counterexample (well-ordering method): (1) Verify S_1; (2) Assume not all S_n are true; (3) Let k>1 be the smallest integer for which S_k is false; (4) Use that S_{k-1} is true (and minimality of k) to derive a contradiction showing S_k must be true.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a hybrid of induction and contradiction that forces a collision between a true earlier case and the falsity of the minimal counterexample, often yielding an explicit contradiction. The method is 'automatic' in many settings; be explicit about minimality and the derived contradiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure enough base cases in induction variants
rubrics_metrics.description: When the inductive argument requires information from several earlier indices (e.g., strong induction that uses S_{k-5}), the base step must verify the initial block of statements up to that offset (e.g., S_1,...,S_6).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check and state clearly which and how many initial cases are established so that the inductive hypothesis is valid for all k in the inductive step. The textbook example with 12 | (n^4 - n^2) checks n=1..6 explicitly because S_{k-5} is used.

rubrics_metrics.name: Using recurrence relations in inductive proofs (Fibonacci pattern)
rubrics_metrics.description: When proving identities or properties of sequences defined by a recurrence (e.g., F_n = F_{n-1}+F_{n-2}), structure the induction to use that recurrence directly in the inductive step.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect to use two base cases when the recurrence references two earlier terms. In the inductive step substitute the recurrence for F_{k+1} or F_{k+2} as needed, then algebraically simplify to match the claimed form (the Fibonacci examples illustrate this).

rubrics_metrics.name: Proving divisibility statements by induction
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove statements of the form 'd divides expression(n)' for all n, express the (k+1)th expression in terms of earlier expressions and show the difference is divisible by d (factor out d or express remainder as multiple of d).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sometimes ordinary induction fails to factor out the modulus; strong induction or verifying several initial cases and using earlier cases (as integers) can allow factoring. Show explicitly an integer multiple of d at the end of algebraic manipulation (e.g., produce 12*(integer)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and checklist for reflexive relations
rubrics_metrics.description: A relation R on set A is reflexive iff x R x for every x ∈ A.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prove reflexivity by taking an arbitrary x ∈ A and demonstrating xRx (often trivially true by definition, e.g., n | 0 gives x ≡ x (mod n)). In diagrams, reflexivity is represented by a loop at each point; for infinite sets use algebraic/divisibility arguments rather than diagrams.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and checklist for symmetric relations
rubrics_metrics.description: A relation R on set A is symmetric iff xRy implies yRx for all x,y ∈ A.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prove symmetry by assuming xRy and deducing yRx (e.g., multiply both sides by -1 in divisibility arguments to swap sign). In diagrams, symmetry is indicated by pairs of arrows in both directions between nodes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and checklist for transitive relations
rubrics_metrics.description: A relation R on set A is transitive iff whenever xRy and yRz, then xRz.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prove by taking arbitrary x,y,z with xRy and yRz and deriving xRz (often by adding or composing the defining relations, e.g., adding divisibility equalities). In diagrams, transitivity corresponds to implied arrows (if x→y and y→z then x→z).

rubrics_metrics.name: Using diagrams vs algebraic proofs for relations
rubrics_metrics.description: Diagrams (arrow/loop pictures) help spot relation properties for small finite relations, but are inadequate for large or infinite relations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use diagrams to visually check reflexivity (loops), symmetry (mutual arrows), and transitivity (composite arrows produce direct arrows). For infinite or arithmetic relations (e.g., congruence mod n), use algebraic proofs based on divisibility and the definitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exploit the semantic meaning of a relation to prove properties
rubrics_metrics.description: If a relation has an interpretable meaning (e.g., 'has same parity', 'are both consonants'), use that meaning to reason about reflexivity, symmetry, transitivity more directly than by brute-force checking ordered pairs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mapping the set-theoretic definition to an intuitive meaning often makes properties obvious (e.g., 'same parity' is reflexive, symmetric and transitive by parity reasoning). Still, formalize the argument with universally quantified statements when needed.
